newsitem.title: CHINA: China seeks to curb official waste, corruption.
newsitem.headline: China seeks to curb official waste, corruption.

text.p: China has sought to curb waste and extravagance in the civil service by re-publishing rules curbing construction of new buildings and threatening corrupt officials with punishment, the People's Daily said on Friday.

The edict, first issued by the State Council, or cabinet, and the Communist Party in May, banned impoverished areas from constructing or buying new government or Communist Party buildings for three years from 1997, the newspaper said.
"Extravagance and waste still exist and it is spreading in some regions and departments," the newspaper said.

The regulations called for severe punishment of Communist Party and government officials who use public funds to pursue extravagant lifestyles, it said, but gave no details of what the penalties would be.
Local authorities were banned from using bank loans to construct or purchase new buildings, and no government or party office buildings should be renovated for three years, it said.
Spending on conferences should be reduced by at least 10 percent this year from the year earlier, and celebrations should be kept to an absolute minimum, the newspaper said.

Spending public funds on extravagant meals, entertainment and trips overseas was forbidden, it said, and officials were banned from using public funds to buy personal mobile telephones and installing telephones at their home.
In the first five months of this year, China exposed 5,431 government or party officials involved in corruption, including embezzlement, bribery and misappropriation of public funds.
Corruption, virtually eliminated in the years after communists took power in 1949, has bounced back in China in the past two decades in the wake of economic reforms.
